SMTO-K8S-0003 — Kubernetes sign-in details were found where they don't belong

GUID: 052d744d-b4f4-4d35-ab73-b5b5ff401a2a
Slug: kubernetes-private-routing-rejected
Domain: K8S · Subsystem: k8s

What happened

  • An older version of SMTO reported Kubernetes sign-in details inside information that is shown openly. The current SMTO no longer makes this check, so the message most likely comes from an older record.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Look at when this error appeared. If it's attached to an older conversation or task, nothing needs to be done now. The current SMTO no longer raises this error, so it usually comes from older records.
  2. If it appears on new Kubernetes work, open Settings › Setup › Gateways and select Check for updates for the Gateway that ran it. LocalMachine is updated together with SMTO itself. An outdated Gateway may still be running the older check.
  3. Ask the person who manages Kubernetes access to keep passwords and tokens only in the sign-in part of the Kubernetes settings, not in cluster or context names. Sign-in details placed in names could be shown openly in SMTO.

What success looks like

  • New Kubernetes commands run without this error appearing.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO. Don't paste Kubernetes tokens or passwords into the conversation.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Legacy diagnostic: private Kubernetes credential material was rejected from public routing metadata; the current kubeconfig collector has retired this check and no current code path raises it.

What this means

  • This retained compatibility definition describes rejected public credential material, but the current private-kubeconfig collector explicitly retires contamination checks and has no direct rejecting producer. These are local configuration/observation checks, not proof of cluster reachability or command rollback. Optional observation failure cannot change the underlying command outcome; diagnostics perform no cluster operations.

Why this can happen

  • This retained compatibility definition describes rejected public credential material, but the current private-kubeconfig collector explicitly retires contamination checks and has no direct rejecting producer.

How to diagnose it

  • Locate the original emitting version and bounded diagnostic before attributing the failure to credential leakage.

How to fix it

  • Use Technical details to find where this code was recorded (an older Server or Gateway build, a saved receipt or a log). Keep Kubernetes credentials in the kubeconfig users section or its exec plugin, never in context, cluster or namespace names, and update older Gateways to the current build.
  • Inspect the original emitting path; use supported private kubeconfig authentication and keep credentials out of public metadata.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • Current supported discovery yields public routing metadata while private authentication remains in its supported store.

What not to do

  • Do not repeatedly submit the same invalid input; correct the named constraint first.

Technical notes

  • These are local configuration/observation checks, not proof of cluster reachability or command rollback. Optional observation failure cannot change the underlying command outcome; diagnostics perform no cluster operations.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
